s0.why: [1] says naturally occurring volcanic glass formed when extruded lava cools rapidly with minimal crystal growth.

s1.why: [4] gives high silica and high viscosity, [5] says viscosity inhibits atom diffusion and nucleation, [6] adds rapid cooling yields glass; 'stops' slightly firms up 'inhibits' but is a fair paraphrase.

s2.why: [7] says hard, brittle and amorphous so it fractures with very sharp edges; [43] says Stone Age cultures valued it for sharp blades or arrowheads.

f0.why: [17] says mainly SiO2, usually 70% by weight or more.

f1.why: [14] says not a true mineral and [15] says it is sometimes classified as a mineraloid.

f2.why: [38] names Kariandusi (Kenya) as the first known archaeological evidence of use, dated 700,000 BC.

f3.why: [34] lists Big Obsidian Flow, 700 acres, in the caldera of Newberry Volcano.

f4.why: [25] says most black obsidians contain nanoinclusions of magnetite.

q1.why: [1], [6] and [10] all tie the glass to rapid cooling with minimal crystal growth, so quick cooling follows.

q2.why: [7] gives the very sharp fracture edges and [43] says it was knapped into sharp blades or arrowheads.

q3.why: [16] says dark like basalt but extremely felsic, [17] gives mainly SiO2, [18] names granite as a crystalline rock of similar composition.

q4.why: [19] says the glass devitrifies into fine-grained crystals over time, so obsidian older than Miocene is rare.

q5.why: [22] says it becomes progressively hydrated by groundwater, forming perlite, and gives the under-1% figure; [21] says water accelerates the transformation.

q6.why: [14] gives both reasons: as a glass it is not crystalline and its composition is too variable.
